paragraphs: More young people are dying on Irish roads this year. Gardaí say 38 people aged 16 to 25 have died so far in 2026. Last year, the number was 26 at this time. That is a rise of almost half.
In total, 151 people have died on the roads this year. That is 12 more than last year. Young people are now one in four of these deaths.
In August, five teenagers died in one crash on the M9 road in Kildare. More passengers are dying too. Their number went up from 10 to 26.
This weekend is a bank holiday, and many people will travel. The police want everyone to be careful on the roads.
The clocks go back on Sunday, so evenings will be dark earlier. People who walk should wear bright clothes so drivers can see them.
The number of young people killed on Irish roads has gone up by almost half this year, according to new figures from the gardaí.

So far in 2026, 38 people aged between 16 and 25 have died on the roads. At the same time last year, the number was 26. This is an increase of 46 per cent. Young people now make up about a quarter of all road deaths.

Altogether, 151 people have been killed on Irish roads this year, which is 12 more than in the same period of 2025. The summer was especially bad, with 21 deaths in July and 22 in August. In August, five teenagers lost their lives in one crash on the M9 motorway in Co Kildare, when a car was driving the wrong way.

The figures show some other changes too. The number of passengers who died rose sharply, from 10 to 26. Fewer motorcyclists were killed, down from 28 to 22. The number of pedestrians who died, 29, is the same as last year, and many of them were over 65.

Denis Ferry, the Garda officer in charge of road safety, asked everyone to take care over the bank holiday weekend. The clocks go back on Sunday, which means it will get dark earlier. Gardaí say more pedestrians are hurt when the days are shorter, so people walking should wear bright clothes.
The Government also wants to improve road safety. Seán Canney, the minister responsible, says a plan to change the Road Safety Authority will be ready in the coming weeks.
Road deaths among young people in Ireland have risen by nearly half this year, according to provisional figures released by An Garda Síochána ahead of the October bank holiday weekend.

The data shows that 38 people aged 16 to 25 have been killed on Irish roads so far in 2026, compared with 26 during the same period last year, an increase of 46 per cent. This age group now accounts for roughly a quarter of all fatalities.

Overall, 151 people have died in road collisions this year, 12 more than at the same point in 2025. The summer months were particularly deadly, with 21 deaths in July and 22 in August. The worst single incident was a wrong-way collision on the M9 in Co Kildare in August, which claimed the lives of five teenagers.

The breakdown reveals other significant trends. Passenger deaths have more than doubled, climbing from 10 to 26, while motorcyclist fatalities fell from 28 to 22. Pedestrian deaths remain unchanged at 29, with people over 65 making up the largest group.

Assistant Commissioner Denis Ferry, who heads roads policing, urged all road users to look out for one another over the long weekend. With the clocks going back on Sunday, he warned that shorter daylight hours are linked to a rise in pedestrian casualties. Earlier this week, gardaí also seized 122 e-scooters, e-bikes and scramblers in a crackdown.
Meanwhile, Minister of State Seán Canney said an implementation plan for reforming the Road Safety Authority would be presented to him within weeks.

According to the data, 38 people aged between 16 and 25 have been killed so far in 2026, up from 26 over the corresponding period last year, a rise of 46 per cent. Young people now account for approximately one in four road fatalities, a disproportionate share for such a narrow age bracket.

The overall death toll stands at 151, a dozen more than at this stage of 2025. The summer proved especially grim, with 21 fatalities in July and 22 in August, the latter month marked by a harrowing wrong-way collision on the M9 in Co Kildare that claimed the lives of five teenagers.

Beneath the headline figures lie some striking shifts. Passenger deaths have surged from 10 to 26, whereas motorcyclist fatalities have declined from 28 to 22. Pedestrian deaths have held steady at 29, with those over 65 forming the most vulnerable cohort.

Assistant Commissioner Denis Ferry, head of roads policing, implored motorists to remain vigilant over the long weekend.
